newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT-Greyhound changing up a gear.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT-Greyhound changing up a gear.

text.p: Australia's national coachline operator Greyhound-Pioneer Australia Ltd, which lost its way after publicly listing three years ago, is getting back on track with new management, new buses and an ambitious business plan.

In its wake are a series of disasters which has seen some former directors committed for trial on alleged insider trading charges that nearly brought the country's oldest tour operator to a crashing halt.
All that is behind the company now, says Greyhound-Pioneer's new chairman and managing director Stephen Jones.
"I hope we've cleaned everything out. I hope and anticipate a better operating result this year," Jones told Reuters after the group's annual meeting in Brisbane.
Greyhound made a loss of A$7.7 million in the year ended June 30, 1996.
Greyhound-Pioneer still faces some major barriers, despite seeking to raise a further A$7.0 million in working capital aimed at cutting back accumulated losses of A$17.5 million.
The latest balance sheet shows A$16.7 million of current liabilities, including accounts payable of A$10.6 million, well above current assets of A$5.8 million.
The accounts also show only A$670,000 in cash on hand at June 30.
Jones declined to comment on exactly what he found when he assumed executive management of Greyhound-Pioneer in July 1995.

Two years earlier, Australian Coachlines Pty Ltd which owned Greyhound Australia and Pioneer Coaches had merged with Bowra Holdings Ltd, owner and operator of Bus Australia, to form Greyhound Pioneer Australia Ltd.
"There were substantial errors in the balance sheet," Jones said. What he found was a coach fleet in disrepair.
"We had to retire some 65 coaches out of a fleet of 370," Jones said.
"Part of the reconstruction process has been the departure of a number of our middle managers," Jones said.
"The fleet is not yet fixed but our Christmas-New Year peak period will be profitable with a 'cobbled together' fleet," he said.

Together with its 60 percent shareholder Retirewise Capital Pty Ltd, Greyhound Pioneer is negotiating to buy 35 new vehicles (costing A$460,000 each) and had hired new management in its workshops, Jones said.
"Minor breakages are no longer evident," he said.
Current trading showed revenue was on the increase and there were "no crises in sight," Jones said.
With 900 destinations daily, often in remote outback areas, Greyhound-Pioneer encourages comparisons with its United States namesake.
Jones said there were several operational tactics of Greyhound US that Greyhound-Pioneer would like to adopt here.
"Greyhound U.S. has come out of Chapter 11 (bankruptcy) and have re-employed experts who understand their locations - that's what we're doing here," he said.
"Greyhound in the U.S. use their terminals as retail outlets and we're trying to convert our terminals to do the same," Jones said.
Greyhound-Pioneer was also talking to the Australian government to try and get wider coaches that were used in the U.S.
These and an innovative plan that would see complete engines able to be changed over in under one hour via a pallet scheme at terminals, would transform the company's operations, Jones said.
"But we have different competitive forces here in Australia," Jones said.
A new information system operating by early next year and monthly profit-and-loss statements will keep costs under tight control, he said.
"We believe Greyhound-Pioneer will be profitable with what we've done," Jones said.
"The extent of that profitability I can't say," he said.
Greyhound's shares were untraded around 2.00 p.m. (0300 GMT), having closed up half a cent at 12 cents on Friday.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
